3. The facts of the original suit in brief are that the suit land belonged to Basir Shah, the maternal grandfather of the plaintiff No. 2 Basir Shah gifted the suit land to the plaintiff No.2. Thereafter Aftabur Reja took khas possession of the 2nd schedule lands by force and then settled it to one Rajob Ali. After the death of Rajob Ali the land lord again took possession of the said land and settled it to Hurmot Ali. Thereafter Hurmot Ali sold the said land to the plaintiff No.1 by registered deed dated 12th July, 1949. Hurmot Ali had two huts but he did not remove the same. Accordingly the plaintiff No.1 instituted Title Suit No.86 of 1950 for recovery of kkhs possession. The suit was disposed of on compromise and the plaintiff No.1 got possession through Court on 4th November, 1951. The defendants tried to cut bamboos from the said land when the plaintiff No.1 instituted a criminal case against him. The defendants threatened the plaintiffs for dispossession in the middle part of Agrahayan, and thereafter the defendants trespassed into the 3rd schedule land out of the 2nd schedule by dispossessing the plaintiffs. 

 8. Mr. Md. Badruddoza, learned Advocate appearing for the appellants contends that the Court of appeal below being the final Court of fact having found that the plain-tiffs predecessor A. Manaf purchased the suit land from Rajob Ali, the predecessor of the defendants, by registered deed dated 15th November, 1938, the defendants can-not acquire title in the suit lands after the death of Rajob Ali and that the defendants having admitted in their written statement that Hnnot Ali, the predecessor of the plaintiffs, was in permissive possession but as they failed to prove their claim of permissive possession, the High Court Division acted illegally in reversing the decision of the lower appellate Court. The learned Counsel further contends that the Court of appeal below having found that the plaintiffs purchased the suit lands from Hunnat Ali by registered deed dated 12th July, 1949 and gotten possession in execution of a decree passed in Title Suit No. 26 of 1950 being Title Execution Case No. 96 of 1951, the plaintiffs title and possession was established but the High Court Division reversed the decision of the lower appellate Court without considering the documentary evidence, such as, exts. 2(ka), 3, 4, 5 series and 6 series. The learned Counsel finally contends that the High Court division erred in law in holding that the plaintiffs could not prove the date of dispossession on a total misreading of the evidence on record in failing to consider that the lower appellate Court on a proper appreciation on evidence on record came to a. definite finding that the defendants dispossessed the plaintiffs in the month of Agrahayan, 1373 B.S. corresponding to 1st part of December, 1966 and that the defendants having not denied the plaintiffs positive statements regarding the date of dispossession, the defendants in fact admitted the plaintiffs claim of dis-possession.
